title: XOR.DDoS_Incident_Response_3ae
description: Investigate and respond to a potential XOR.DDoS malware incident on Linux servers.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The organization has detected unusual network activity on its Linux servers. Initial analysis suggests the presence of the Groundhog backdoor malware, which is associated with the XOR.DDoS malware family. Your task is to investigate and respond to this potential security incident.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
You have SSH access to the target server with the following credentials:
- Host: target (192.168.50.5)
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

Enter 'start' to begin the scenario.
levels.local_content:
Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario. Use the following credentials to access the target server:
- Host: target (192.168.50.5)
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

Enter 'start' to begin the scenario.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Network Activity
levels.content: While monitoring network traffic, you noticed unusual outbound connections from the target server. Investigate this activity and identify any suspicious services or processes that might be responsible. Enter the port number of the suspicious service.
levels.solution: Check running services and network connections. The suspicious service is running on port 4444.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Start by examining the system's active network connections and running services.

hints.title: Actionable Hint
hints.content: Use the command 'netstat -tuln' to list all active network connections and 'ps aux' to list running processes.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Look for any unfamiliar or unexpected services listening on network ports.

levels.title: Analyze Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Now that you've identified the suspicious service, determine how it maintains persistence on the system. Investigate the system's startup configuration to find any unauthorized entries. Enter the name of the systemd timer responsible for the service's persistence.
levels.solution: Check systemd services and timers. The systemd timer responsible for the service's persistence is lab-checkin.timer.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Persistence mechanisms often involve system startup configurations.

hints.title: Actionable Hint
hints.content: Use the command 'systemctl list-timers --all' to list all systemd timers.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Look for any unfamiliar or recently modified timers that might be related to the suspicious service.

levels.title: Investigate Lateral Movement
levels.content: The attacker might be using this server as a foothold to move laterally within the network. Investigate any evidence of file transfers or remote execution that could indicate lateral movement. Enter the name of the service responsible for lateral movement.
levels.solution: Check for any scripts or services that transfer files to other hosts. The payload-transfer service and its associated timer are responsible for lateral movement.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Lateral movement often involves file transfers or remote execution.

hints.title: Actionable Hint
hints.content: Use the command 'systemctl list-units --type=service' to list all systemd services.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Look for any services that transfer files to other hosts or execute commands remotely.
